s: Which institution provides buyers' and sellers' credit and lines of credit to promote exports?
x: EXIM Bank provides lines of credit and buyers'/sellers' credit; ECGC gives export credit insurance and DGFT issues FTP authorisations.

s:
Consider the following statements about EXIM Bank:
1. It provides lines of credit, buyer's/seller's credit and project-export finance.
2. Export credit insurance is its principal role.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: EXIM Bank gives such finance, but export credit insurance is ECGC's role, so statement 2 is wrong.

s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: ECGC – Government-owned export credit insurance company
MMTC – Trading in minerals, metals and precious metals
NIRVIK – ECGC scheme enhancing insurance cover on export credit
STC – Export credit insurance cover scheme
x: STC (1956) is a canalising agency for bulk commodities; export credit insurance is ECGC's role.

s: In which year was the Export Credit Guarantee Corporation (ECGC) set up?
x: ECGC dates from 1957; STC from 1956, EXIM Bank from 1982 and IBEF from 1996.

s: In which year was the State Trading Corporation (STC), a canalising agency for bulk goods, set up?
x: STC was set up in 1956; ECGC came in 1957.

s: Under the present Foreign Trade Policy, how are status holders recognised on the basis of export performance?
o: As Export Houses and Trading Houses only
As One-Star to Five-Star Export Houses
x: Status holders are now graded as One-Star to Five-Star Export Houses according to their export performance.

s: Which is the largest trading government company in India?
x: MMTC, which deals in minerals and metals, is India's largest trading government company.

s: Where is the EXIM Bank of India headquartered?
x: EXIM Bank was set up on 1 January 1982 at Mumbai under the EXIM Bank Act 1981.

s: What is the full form of NIRVIK?
o: National Initiative for Rural Value-added Industrial Kits
x: NIRVIK = Niryat Rin Vikas Yojana, giving higher ECGC insurance cover to exporters.

s: Where is the office of the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) located?
x: DGFT, an attached office of the Department of Commerce, is at Vanijya Bhavan, New Delhi.

s: RoDTEP replaced which WTO-challenged scheme of FTP 2015–20?
x: RoDTEP replaced the WTO-challenged Merchandise Exports from India Scheme (MEIS) of FTP 2015–20.

s: Under the Foreign Trade Policy 2015-20, what did MEIS and SEIS respectively relate to?
x: MEIS provided support for exports of goods, while SEIS related to exports of services under FTP 2015-20.

s: RoDTEP replaced which scheme and seeks to refund which category of burden?
o: SEIS; only income tax paid by exporters
MEIS; unrebated central, state and local taxes
RoSL; only customs duties on imported inputs
x: RoDTEP replaced MEIS and refunds unrebated central, state and local taxes, including electricity duty and VAT on transport fuel.

s: RoSCTL replaced RoSL. For which goods does it mainly provide a rebate?
x: RoSCTL replaced RoSL and provides a rebate for apparel and made-ups.

s: Which body runs the Export Promotion Mission, aimed at MSMEs and first-time exporters?
x: DGFT runs the Export Promotion Mission, which merges Interest Equalisation and the Market Access Initiative.

s: For what does the RELIEF Scheme 2026, implemented through ECGC, mainly provide support?
o: Interest subsidy on domestic housing loans
War-risk and logistics costs in West Asia
x: RELIEF Scheme 2026 provides support for war-risk and logistics costs in West Asia through ECGC under the Export Promotion Mission.

s: What does Advance Authorisation permit?
o: Duty-free import of inputs for export production
Refund of income tax on exports
x: Advance Authorisation is for inputs; EPCG is for capital goods.

s: Which of the following is NOT refunded under duty drawback?
x: Duty drawback refunds duties and service tax on inputs used in exports, never income tax.

s: What is the outlay of the Export Promotion Mission (FY 2025-26 to 2030-31)?
x: The Export Promotion Mission has ₹25,060 crore; ₹497 crore is the RELIEF Scheme.

s: For whom is the Export Promotion Mission mainly meant?
o: Large exporters and star export houses
x: The Export Promotion Mission (Rs 25,060 crore), run by DGFT, is aimed at MSMEs and first-time exporters.

s: Which body runs the RoDTEP scheme online?
x: RoDTEP refunds are run online by the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC).

s: What does the Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) scheme allow?
o: Duty-free import of inputs for export production
Refund of VAT on transport fuel
Zero-duty import of capital goods against an export obligation
x: EPCG allows zero-duty import of capital goods against an export obligation; Advance Authorisation covers inputs.

s: Which two schemes were merged into the Export Promotion Mission?
o: Interest Equalisation Scheme and Market Access Initiative
x: The Export Promotion Mission merges the Interest Equalisation Scheme and the Market Access Initiative.

s: Which department frames and monitors India's Foreign Trade Policy?
x: The Department of Commerce frames and monitors India's Foreign Trade Policy.

s: What was the Foreign Trade Policy target for India's share in world services exports by 2022?
x: The Foreign Trade Policy had set a target of 4.2% for India's share in world services exports by 2022.

s: What is the export target of the Foreign Trade Policy 2023 for 2030?
x: FTP 2023, in effect from 1 April 2023 with no fixed end date, targets US$ 2 trillion of exports by 2030.

s: 'Districts as Export Hubs' is a pillar of which policy?
x: Districts as Export Hubs is one of the pillars of FTP 2023.

s: Which of the following is NOT a pillar of the Foreign Trade Policy 2023?
x: MEIS belonged to FTP 2015-20 and was replaced by RoDTEP; the other three are FTP 2023 pillars.

s: Which of the following Foreign Trade Policies has no fixed end date?
x: FTP 2023 came into force on 1 April 2023 with no end date.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about India's trade policy history?
o: The 1991 Trade Policy shifted to a price-based regime
Foreign Trade Policy replaced EXIM Policy in 1991
x: Foreign Trade Policy replaced the EXIM Policy from 2004, not 1991; the other three are correct.

s: Under the partial current-account convertibility of 1992, how were foreign exchange transactions divided?
o: 60% at the official rate and 40% at the market rate
50% at the official rate and 50% at the market rate
20% at the official rate and 80% at the market rate
40% at the official rate and 60% at the market rate
x: In 1992, partial current-account convertibility provided for 40% of foreign exchange at the official rate and 60% at the market rate.

s: Under which Ministry is the Foreign Trade Policy administered through the Directorate General of Foreign Trade?
o: Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises
x: The Foreign Trade Policy is administered by the Department of Commerce, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, through the DGFT.

s: When did the Foreign Trade Policy 2023 come into force?
x: FTP 2023 came into force on 1 April 2023 and has no fixed end date.

s: Up to what date was the Foreign Trade Policy 2015-20 extended?
x: FTP 2015-20 was extended (COVID-19, geopolitics) till 31 March 2023; FTP 2023 began on 1 April 2023.

s: Which of the following is a feature of the Foreign Trade Policy 2023?
o: A shift from remission and entitlement support to only quantitative restrictions
A shift from incentives towards remission and entitlement-based support
A complete withdrawal of electronic initiatives
x: FTP 2023 shifts the emphasis from conventional incentives towards remission and entitlement-based support, while also promoting e-initiatives and merchanting trade.

s: Under which schemes does FTP 2023 offer a one-time amnesty for export-obligation defaults?
x: FTP 2023 includes a one-time amnesty for EPCG and Advance Authorisation export-obligation defaults, along with rupee trade settlement and new Towns of Export Excellence.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Foreign Trade Policy 2023:
1. It came into force on 1 April 2023.
2. It has a fixed end date of 31 March 2028.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: FTP 2023 began on 1 April 2023 and has no fixed end date.

s: What is the export target set by the Foreign Trade Policy 2023?
x: FTP 2023 targets $2 trillion exports by 2030; the $1 trillion goal was a July 2026 remark.

s: Along with rupee trade settlement, which kind of trade does the Foreign Trade Policy 2023 promote?
x: FTP 2023 promotes international trade in INR and merchanting trade.

s: Which export-import document is the customs document for clearing export goods?
x: The shipping bill clears export goods through customs; a letter of credit is the importer's bank guarantee of payment.

s: What do rules of origin mainly determine?
o: The international price of a product
The amount of countervailing duty payable
The national source of a product
x: Rules of origin establish the national source of a product and help determine eligibility for free-trade agreement concessions.

s: Which export document is issued by a ship's mate to acknowledge that goods have been loaded on board?
x: The mate's receipt confirms the goods are loaded on board; the bill of lading is the shipping company's receipt and document of title.

s: In export-import trade, what is an indent?
o: The shipping company's document of title
The customs document for export goods
The importer's order to buy goods
The ship's mate's acknowledgement of loading
x: An indent is the importer's order to buy goods.

s: What does a bill of lading serve as?
o: A shipping company’s receipt and a document of title to the goods
An exporter’s application for a duty drawback
A customs order fixing the tariff rate
x: A bill of lading is the shipping company’s receipt and also functions as a document of title to the goods.

s: Which is the nodal agency for Agri Export Zones in India?
x: The Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA) is the nodal agency for Agri Export Zones.

s: Which body handles the export promotion of marine products?
x: MPEDA handles marine products; APEDA (under the Department of Commerce) handles agricultural exports.

s: Where was India's first Agriculture Export Facilitation Centre set up in May 2021?
x: The first Agriculture Export Facilitation Centre was opened at Pune in May 2021.

s: What was the main aim of the Agriculture Export Policy 2018?
o: To replace APEDA with a new board
To set up SEZs only for farm goods
x: The Agriculture Export Policy 2018 aimed to double India's agri exports.

s: What is ICEGATE?
o: A postal export network of India Post
A logistics ranking index of NITI Aayog
A single-window system for foreign investment approvals
A customs e-filing portal of CBIC
x: ICEGATE is the customs e-filing portal of the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC).

s: APEDA, the nodal agency for Agri Export Zones, functions under which Ministry?
x: APEDA is under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, not Agriculture.

s: When was the APEDA Act passed?
x: The APEDA Act was passed in December 1985 and came into force on 13 February 1986.

s: To what level did the Agriculture Export Policy 2018 aim to raise agri exports?
x: The 2018 policy aimed to double agri exports to about $60 bn by 2022.

s: In which year was India's first Agriculture Export Facilitation Centre set up at Pune?
x: The first Agriculture Export Facilitation Centre was set up at Pune in May 2021.

s: The SWIFT system in the context of trade facilitation is associated with which function?
x: SWIFT functions as a single window for import clearance.

s: In which year was the National Logistics Policy, aimed at cutting logistics costs, launched?
x: The National Logistics Policy came in 2022; PM Gati Shakti came in 2021.

s: In LEADS 2025, Andhra Pradesh was placed in which category among coastal states?
x: AP was an Accelerator among coastal states; Tamil Nadu was the Exemplar.

s: In which year was PM Gati Shakti launched to cut logistics costs?
x: PM Gati Shakti was launched in 2021; the National Logistics Policy followed in 2022.

s: Which body releases the LEADS (Logistics Ease Across Different States) index?
o: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways
x: LEADS 2025, the 7th edition, was released by DPIIT on 13 May 2026.

s: In LEADS 2025, which coastal state was placed in the 'Exemplar' category?
x: In LEADS 2025, Tamil Nadu was an Exemplar while Andhra Pradesh was an Accelerator.

s: What does import substitution mean?
o: Increasing dependence on imported capital goods
Promoting only agricultural exports through export subsidies
Reducing import dependence by producing import substitutes at home
x: Import substitution is an inward-looking strategy aimed at producing goods domestically in order to reduce import dependency.

s: Which of the following trade policy instruments is a quantitative restriction?
x: An import quota sets a ceiling on the quantity of a good that may be imported, so it is a quantitative restriction. An ad valorem tariff is a tax on the value of imports. Countervailing and anti-dumping duties are also price-based duties, not quantity limits.

s: Free internal trade together with a common external tariff is the feature of which of the following?
x: A customs union adds a common external tariff to free internal trade; an FTA lets members keep their own external tariffs.

s: What does a common market add to a customs union?
o: Free movement of factors of production
x: A customs union has free internal trade and a common external tariff; a common market adds free movement of factors.

s: For trade and tariff purposes, how is a duty-free enclave in an SEZ treated?
o: A bonded warehouse under State control
x: A duty-free enclave is treated as foreign territory for trade and tariff purposes, though it lies within India.

s: Which of the following pairs relating to Special Economic Zones is correctly matched?
o: SEZ effect on employment – Reduction in jobs
SEZ effect on investment – Discourages investment
SEZ effect on infrastructure – Slows infrastructure growth
x: SEZs offer simplified procedures and a business-friendly environment, which boosts exports, investment, jobs and infrastructure.

s: Which of the following pairs relating to SEZs is correctly matched?
x: The SEZ concept came in EXIM Policy 1997–2002; the policy was announced in April 2000, the Act enacted in 2005 and the Rules notified in 2006.

s: Where was India's first Export Processing Zone set up in 1965?
x: Kandla (Gujarat) got India's first EPZ in 1965. Santacruz (Mumbai), Falta (West Bengal) and Visakhapatnam got EPZs later, and these were converted into SEZs after the 2000 SEZ policy.

s: What was the objective of the Special Economic Zone Policy in relation to the business environment?
o: To establish a mixed economic model
To provide an internationally competitive environment
To create a long-term fiscal policy
x: One SEZ objective was an internationally competitive business environment. Licensing and the mixed economy belong to older policies.

s: In which year was the Special Economic Zones Act enacted?
x: SEZ policy came on 1 April 2000, the SEZ Act in 2005 and SEZ Rules in 2006.

s: In which year was the Special Economic Zone (SEZ) Policy announced in India?
x: The SEZ Policy was announced on 1 April 2000; the SEZ Act came in 2005 and the Rules in 2006.

s: EOUs, EHTPs and STPs are units that:
o: Export at least half of their output
Pay full customs duty on inputs
Must be located only in SEZs
x: These units export all their output, may be located anywhere and get duty-free inputs.

s: Up to what limit is FDI in most manufacturing in SEZs allowed under the automatic route?
x: 100 per cent FDI is allowed under the automatic route for most manufacturing; SEZs are governed by the SEZ Act, 2005.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: SEZ — units that must be located anywhere outside a designated enclave
x: B is correct: EHTP units deal in electronics hardware and get duty-free inputs. EOUs cover goods generally (not only software), STPs cover software (not agricultural machinery), and an SEZ is itself a designated duty-free enclave, whereas it is EOU/EHTP/STP units that can be located anywhere.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about export units?
o: An SEZ is treated as foreign territory
EOUs must be located within an SEZ
x: EOUs, EHTPs and STPs can be located anywhere; only an SEZ is an enclave.

s: Under Districts as Export Hubs, what does each district's plan prioritise?
x: Each district's export plan prioritises 2-3 high-potential products or services.

s: Which of the following is NOT an AP priority district in the 90-day Districts as Export Hubs campaign from 1 June 2026?
x: The priority districts are Ananthapur, Chittoor, East Godavari, Guntur, Krishna and Visakhapatnam; Srikakulam is not one.

s: Under Districts as Export Hubs, in how many districts had export products been identified by 2025?
x: Products were identified in 734 districts and action plans prepared for 590 (2025).

s: How does the IMF presentation of the Balance of Payments differ from that generally followed by the RBI?
o: The IMF uses only current and capital accounts, whereas the RBI uses current, capital and financial accounts separately.
The IMF uses only trade and services accounts, whereas the RBI uses current and financial accounts.
The IMF uses current, capital and financial accounts, whereas the RBI generally combines the capital and financial accounts.
Both the IMF and the RBI invariably present the Balance of Payments through exactly three separate accounts.
x: Under BPM6, the IMF distinguishes current, capital and financial accounts. The RBI generally combines the capital and financial accounts under the heading ‘capital account’.

s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Balance of Trade covers only goods or visible trade.
A Balance of Trade deficit occurs when goods imports exceed goods exports.
Balance of Trade is the complete record of economic transactions with the rest of the world.
A Balance of Trade surplus occurs when goods exports exceed goods imports.
x: Option C is incorrect: the full record of transactions with the world is the balance of payments. The balance of trade covers only goods.

s: In the IMF's BPM6 presentation, how many main accounts does the Balance of Payments have?
x: BPM6 uses three accounts (current, capital, financial); the RBI combines capital and financial as the 'Capital Account'.

s: Which of the following is NOT included among the components of India’s foreign exchange reserves?
x: India’s foreign exchange reserves include Foreign Currency Assets, gold, SDRs and the reserve position in the IMF. Fiscal deficit deposits are not a reserve component.

s: Which is the largest component of India's foreign exchange reserves?
x: Foreign Currency Assets are the largest component ($597.6 bn on 9 Oct 2026); gold is second.

s: How many months of import cover did India's forex reserves of $682.3 billion (29 May 2026) provide?
x: $682.3 bn on 29 May 2026 equalled about 11 months of import cover.

s: At its all-time high of $785.71 billion (15 Sep 2026), what was India's rank among forex reserve holders?
x: India was 4th, after China, Japan and Switzerland.

s: What is a member's Reserve Tranche Position, a component of forex reserves?
o: Conditional loan from the World Bank
Unconditional drawing right from its IMF quota
x: The reserve tranche is an unconditional drawing right from the member's IMF quota.

s: In which year did India's foreign exchange reserves first cross US$ 100 billion?
x: India's forex reserves crossed US$ 100 billion in December 2003.

s: Which RBI step drove India's overall BoP surplus of $20.8 bn in July 2026?
x: The RBI's special FCNR(B) deposit scheme drew NRI deposits and gave a $20.8 bn overall BoP surplus.

s: A Current Account Deficit occurs when payments exceed receipts from which of the following?
o: Goods, services, transfers and net income
x: The current account has visible trade plus invisibles (services, transfers, net income); a CAD means payments on these exceed receipts.

s: During which period did India record a current account surplus for three consecutive years?
x: India had current account surpluses for three consecutive years from 2001-02 to 2003-04.

s: Which of the following is a cyclical, not structural, cause of India's current account deficit?
o: Dependence on imported oil and gold
x: A temporary global slowdown is cyclical; oil and gold imports, weak export competitiveness and the savings-investment gap are structural.

s: When did India's current account deficit reach its peak of about 4.8% of GDP?
o: 1990-91, during the balance of payments crisis
FY24, after the fall in imports
H1 FY26, after the US tariffs
x: The CAD peaked at about 4.8% of GDP in FY13, the taper tantrum period. In the 1990-91 crisis it was about 3.1-3.2% of GDP. FY24 saw a recovery, with a surplus in Q4, and H1 FY26 had a CAD of only 0.8% of GDP.

s: In which year did India record its first current account surplus in 24 years?
x: 2001-02 brought the first surplus in 24 years, beginning the 2001-02 to 2003-04 run; 2004-05 turned to deficit.

s: What was India's current account deficit for FY 2025-26?
x: FY 2025-26 CAD was $25.2 bn, about 0.6% of GDP; $4.2 bn (0.5%) was Q1 2026-27 and $13.2 bn (1.3%) was Q3 FY26.

s: Which is correct about India's peak CAD of 4.8% of GDP in FY13?
o: It was lower than the 1990-91 crisis level
It was a current account surplus
It was higher than the 1990-91 crisis level of 3.1-3.2%
It occurred during the 1991 BoP crisis
x: The FY13 peak of 4.8% (taper tantrum) exceeded the 1990-91 crisis CAD of 3.1-3.2% of GDP.

s: What led to India's external-sector recovery in FY 2023-24?
o: A sharp rise in merchandise exports
A sharp fall in import growth along with moderate export growth
A rise in net primary income
x: In FY24 merchandise export growth moderated but import growth fell sharply, and services exports cushioned the deficit.

s: What was India's current account deficit in Q1 2026-27?
x: Q1 2026-27 CAD was $4.2 bn, 0.5% of GDP, against $3.4 bn (0.4%) a year earlier.

s: To what level did India's services exports rise in FY 2023-24?
x: Services exports rose 4.85% to USD 341.06 bn in FY 2023-24, cushioning the deficit.

s: The record services surplus of $188.8 billion in FY25 financed approximately what proportion of the merchandise deficit?
x: The record services surplus of $188.8 billion in FY25 financed about two-thirds of the merchandise deficit. Remittances also acted as a cushion.

s: India was estimated to be the world's largest recipient of remittances in FY25. What was the approximate amount of remittances and their share in India's GDP, respectively?
x: India received approximately $135.4 billion in remittances in FY25, equivalent to about 3.5% of its GDP.

s: Why are remittances significant for India's external sector?
o: They are counter-cyclical and do not create a debt burden or repayment obligation.
They are classified entirely as foreign direct investment inflows.
They can be received only through external commercial borrowings.
They are pro-cyclical and create a direct repayment obligation for the recipient country.
x: Remittances are counter-cyclical and do not create a repayment obligation, unlike debt-related flows such as ECBs or certain portfolio liabilities.

s: Which country sends the largest share (27.7%) of remittances to India?
x: The USA sends the largest share, 27.7% of India's remittances.

s: According to the World Bank, which country was the second-largest remittance recipient in 2024, after India?
x: India ($129 bn) led, followed by Mexico ($68 bn), China ($48 bn), Philippines ($40 bn) and Pakistan ($33 bn).

s: Which is the largest part of India's services surplus?
x: Software services form the largest part of the record $188.8 bn services surplus of FY25.

s: Which of the following items is a net outflow in India's invisibles?
x: Net primary income (interest, dividends, profits) is an outflow for India, while services and remittances bring net inflows.

s: According to the RBI's remittances survey for 2023-24, which country was the second-largest source of remittances to India?
x: The RBI survey ranked USA (27.7%) first, UAE (19.2%) second and UK (10.8%) third in 2023-24.

s: Which country's share in remittances to India rose to 10.8% in 2023-24, making it the third-largest source?
x: The UK's share rose from 6.8% (2021-22) to 10.8% (2023-24), third after USA and UAE.

s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Current Account includes visible trade involving exports and imports of goods.
Foreign Direct Investment is included in the Current Account.
The Capital Account includes foreign loans, FDI and portfolio investment.
The Current Account includes services, transfer payments and net income as invisible transactions.
x: Option B is incorrect: FDI is a capital flow, so it goes in the capital account with foreign loans and portfolio investment. The current account has goods, services, transfers and income.

s: Which of the following is wrongly matched?
o: Balance of Trade – Exports of goods minus imports of goods
Balance of Payments – Complete record of transactions with the rest of the world
Capital Account – Includes the Balance of Trade
Current Account – Includes the Balance of Trade
x: The capital account covers cross-border capital movements; it is the current account that includes the Balance of Trade.

s: The balance of the current account is represented by which of the following expressions?
o: Exports minus imports of goods and services plus net primary and net secondary income
Capital inflows minus capital outflows plus errors and omissions
Exports and imports of goods only plus changes in foreign exchange reserves
Foreign direct investment plus portfolio investment minus external debt
x: The current-account balance equals exports minus imports of goods and services, plus net primary income and net secondary income.

s: Under which head are software services exports recorded in India's Balance of Payments?
x: Software exports are invisible services in the current account; foreign loans go to the capital account and crude oil imports to merchandise trade.

s: How are shipping, banking, tourism and software classified in the balance of payments?
x: These are non-factor services, part of invisibles along with primary (factor) income and transfers.

s: How is the purchase of foreign assets by residents recorded in the capital account?
o: A current-account credit because assets are goods
A debit because foreign exchange flows out for acquiring the assets
A credit because foreign exchange enters the country
x: Purchase of foreign assets by residents is a capital-account debit. Conversely, sale of Indian assets to foreigners is recorded as a credit.

s: Under which account are NRI deposits such as FCNR(B) recorded in India's BoP?
x: NRI deposits are banking capital in the capital (and financial) account.

s: How is a gift sent by an Indian resident to a foreigner recorded in the BoP?
x: Gifts are secondary-income transfers in the current account; a gift to foreigners is a payment, so a debit.

s: Under which part of the current account are private remittances recorded?
x: Remittances, gifts and grants are secondary income (current transfers) in the current account.

s: Which of the following correctly represents the Balance of Payments identity?
o: Current balance + capital balance + financial balance + errors and omissions = zero
Current balance + merchandise exports = financial balance
Current balance − capital balance = trade balance
x: The Balance of Payments identity is current balance plus capital balance plus financial balance plus errors and omissions equal to zero.

s: What is the usual effect of the overall balance of payments position on foreign exchange reserves?
o: The overall balance has no relationship with reserve movements.
A positive overall balance reduces reserves, while a negative balance increases them.
A positive overall balance adds to reserves, while a negative balance draws them down.
Both positive and negative balances increase reserves because the BoP always balances in accounting terms.
x: A positive overall balance adds to foreign exchange reserves, whereas a negative overall balance draws them down. If reserves become insufficient, a balance of payments crisis may result.

s: In the balance of payments, reserve changes and official borrowing are examples of which transactions?
x: Accommodating transactions such as reserve changes and official borrowing fill the gap left by autonomous transactions.

s: Which item closes the BoP accounting identity so that the accounts sum to zero?
x: Current + capital + financial account + net errors and omissions = 0.

s:
Consider the following statements about the balance of payments identity:
1. The BoP always balances in accounting terms.
2. The balance of trade must also always balance.
3. A surplus in one account is matched by a deficit in another.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The BoP always balances, with a surplus in one account offsetting a deficit in another; the balance of trade need not balance.

s: Which additional recommendation was associated with the High Level Committee on Balance of Payments headed by C. Rangarajan?
o: A permanently fixed exchange rate determined by the IMF
Replacement of the current account by the capital account
x: Along with identifying a sustainable CAD of about 1.6% of GDP, the committee recommended a market-determined exchange rate.

s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes FERA from FEMA?
o: FERA was a restrictive criminal law, whereas FEMA is a liberal civil law concerned with management and regulation
FERA followed a liberal approach, whereas FEMA imposed strict control over outflow
FERA was a civil law, whereas FEMA was a criminal law
Both FERA and FEMA were identical in nature and approach
x: FERA 1973 was restrictive and criminal in nature, focusing on control of foreign exchange outflow. FEMA 1999 is a civil law based on management and regulation with a more liberal approach.

s: How did India achieve full current account convertibility in August 1994?
o: Setting up the second Tarapore Committee
Accepting Article VIII of the IMF
x: Full current account convertibility was achieved in August 1994 when India accepted the obligations under Article VIII of the IMF.

s: What did the dual exchange rate under the Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS) comprise?
x: LERMS, introduced in the 1992-93 Budget, used a dual rate of 40% official and 60% market.

s: What level of current account deficit did the High Level Committee on Balance of Payments (C. Rangarajan, 1991-93) regard as sustainable?
x: The C. Rangarajan Committee placed a sustainable CAD at approximately 1.6% of GDP and also recommended a market-determined exchange rate.

s: When did FEMA, which replaced FERA, come into force?
x: FEMA was enacted in 1999 and came into force on 1 June 2000.

s: Who chaired the 1997 Committee on Capital Account Convertibility?
x: S.S. Tarapore chaired both the 1997 committee and the 2006 committee on fuller capital account convertibility.

s:
Consider the following statements about rupee convertibility:
1. India has full current account convertibility.
2. The rupee is fully convertible on the capital account.
3. Current account convertibility came with acceptance of IMF Article VIII.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Full current account convertibility came in August 1994 under Article VIII; the capital account is still only partially convertible.

s: When was the Indian rupee delinked from the pound sterling?
x: In September 1975 the rupee was delinked from sterling and pegged to a basket of currencies.

s: In which year was the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA) enacted?
x: FERA was enacted in 1973; FEMA replaced it in 1999 (in force 2000).

s: Which of the following is an expenditure-switching measure for correcting a BoP deficit?
x: Devaluation, like import tariffs and export incentives, switches demand from foreign to domestic goods; the others reduce expenditure.

s: Which of the following is an expenditure-reducing measure for correcting a BoP deficit?
o: Tight monetary policy through higher interest rates
x: Tight monetary policy reduces aggregate expenditure and imports; devaluation, import substitution and export promotion are expenditure-switching.

s: How is an increase in import duty on gold, used to reduce external pressure, classified?
x: A higher import duty makes imported gold less attractive and helps switch demand towards domestic alternatives or away from imports. It is therefore an expenditure-switching measure.

s: What did the Rekhi Committee (1992) deal with?
x: The Rekhi Committee (1992) was on indirect taxes, not export-import simplification.

s: What kind of measure is a tight monetary policy with higher interest rates, used to correct a BoP deficit?
x: Tight money is expenditure-reducing; devaluation and tariffs are expenditure-switching.

s: Which measure does NOT ordinarily correct a BoP deficit, because it raises demand and imports?
o: Increasing government spending on domestic projects
x: Higher government spending raises demand and imports, so it does not correct a BoP deficit; devaluation, import duties and tight money can help.

s: Which of the following is an IMF lending window for balance of payments support?
x: The Extended Fund Facility (like the Stand-By Arrangement) is an IMF window; RBI's swap facilities and SRVAs are not IMF instruments.

s: A country whose reserves cannot cover its Balance of Payments deficit may approach which institution as lender of last resort?
x: The IMF assists a country that cannot cover its external deficit from its reserves and other sources.

s: Which of the following pairs relating to the IMF is wrongly matched?
o: Reserve Tranche – Unconditional drawing right from quota subscription
Rapid Financing Instrument – Rapid assistance for urgent BoP needs
Rapid Credit Facility – Concessional assistance to Low-Income Countries
IMF core function – Concessional lending to Low-Income Countries
x: The IMF's core function is surveillance, i.e., monitoring global and member economies; concessional help to LICs is the RCF.

s: To which countries does the IMF's Rapid Credit Facility (RCF) provide concessional support?
o: Any member with an urgent BoP need
x: RCF is concessional, for low-income countries; the Rapid Financing Instrument is open to any member.

s: Which of the following is NOT an IMF facility?
x: Special Rupee Vostro Accounts (like RBI swaps) are not IMF instruments; the others are IMF lending windows.

s: How many currencies make up the SDR valuation basket?
x: The SDR is valued on a basket of 5 currencies: US dollar, euro, renminbi, yen and pound sterling.

s: Which currency has the largest weight (43.38%) in the SDR basket?
x: From 1 Aug 2022 the US dollar weighs 43.38%, ahead of the euro at 29.31%.

s: Which of the following pairs (SDR basket currency – weight) is correctly matched?
x: Renminbi weighs 12.28%; the dollar 43.38%, euro 29.31%, yen 7.59% and pound 7.44%.

s: In 1991, India drew on which institution to tide over its balance of payments crisis?
x: India approached the IMF, the lender for BoP difficulties, during the 1991 crisis.

s: Which IMF reserve asset exists only as book-keeping entries and is not a currency in circulation?
x: SDRs, created by the IMF in 1969, exist only as book-keeping entries in IMF records.

s: Why are FCNR(B) deposits and external commercial borrowings viewed cautiously in discussions on India's external-sector sustainability?
o: They are domestic tax receipts and do not affect the balance of payments.
They are temporary inflows, whereas FDI is expected to support a self-sustaining capital surplus.
They are permanent grants and therefore cannot reverse suddenly.
They are components of merchandise exports and reduce the trade deficit directly.
x: FCNR(B) and ECB inflows are considered temporary sources of financing. The preferred long-term basis for a self-sustaining capital surplus is stronger FDI.

s: Which of the following increases a country's external vulnerability?
o: Adequate forex reserves for import cover
Reduced reliance on volatile FPI and debt flows
x: Greater dependence on hot money increases vulnerability; adequate reserves, low short-term debt and less volatile flows are safeguards.

s: During the 2013 taper tantrum, Morgan Stanley included India in which group?
x: Morgan Stanley described India as one of the ‘Fragile Five’ during the 2013 taper tantrum because of external-sector vulnerability.

s: How do increases in US Federal Reserve interest rates and a strong US dollar generally affect emerging markets such as India?
o: They automatically increase India’s net FDI
They raise US yields, attract hot money away from emerging markets and weaken the rupee
They reduce US yields and cause capital to flow into emerging markets
They eliminate exchange-rate volatility in emerging markets
x: US rate hikes and a strong dollar raise US yields, encouraging hot-money outflows from emerging markets and putting downward pressure on the rupee.

s: What was India's external debt-to-GDP ratio at end-June 2026?
x: Debt-to-GDP was 20.8% (from 20.9%); 19.7% was short-term debt's share of total debt.

s: Which currency had the largest share in India's external debt at end-June 2026?
x: The US dollar accounted for 54.8% of external debt, ahead of the rupee at 29.8%.

s: How much did Foreign Portfolio Investors pull out of India in FY 2025-26?
x: FPIs pulled out $16.4 bn in FY26, while net FDI was only $6.9 bn.

s: What was India's total external debt at end-June 2026?
x: External debt was $778.2 bn at end-June 2026, 20.8% of GDP.

s: Which of the following can limit the improvement in the trade balance after a currency depreciation?
x: Depreciation can cause imported inflation, makes inelastic oil imports costlier and raises ECB repayment costs.

s: Why is devaluation described as an expenditure-switching policy?
o: Raises export prices in foreign currency and lowers import prices
Makes imports cheaper and encourages spending on foreign goods
Makes domestic goods cheaper for foreigners and imports costlier for domestic consumers
Eliminates the need for fiscal and monetary measures
x: Devaluation makes home-produced goods relatively cheaper for foreigners and imported goods costlier at home, thereby switching expenditure towards domestic production.

s:
Assertion (A): Devaluation necessarily improves the trade balance.
Reason (R): Devaluation makes exports relatively cheaper.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
x: A is false and R is true: devaluation makes exports cheaper, but it does not always improve the trade balance, since import costs rise too. 'Necessarily' makes A false.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about devaluation?
o: It tends to improve the balance of trade
It raises the foreign-currency prices of exports
It makes imports costlier at home
x: Devaluation lowers, not raises, export prices in foreign-currency terms; that is why it tends to improve the balance of trade.

s: What does a direct exchange-rate quotation express?
o: The annual percentage change in the exchange rate
Units of foreign currency per one unit of domestic currency
The number of months of import cover
Units of domestic currency per one unit of foreign currency
x: A direct quote states the amount of domestic currency required for one unit of foreign currency, such as ₹95 = $1.

s: What does the term 'exchange rate' refer to?
o: The price/value of one currency expressed in terms of another currency
The official reduction in currency value under a fixed exchange-rate system
The weighted average of real exchange rates against trading partners
The market-driven rise in the value of a currency
x: The exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. The other options describe devaluation, REER and appreciation.

s: An importer enters into a forward contract primarily for which purpose?
o: To increase the country's import cover automatically
To cover exchange-rate risk by fixing a rate for a future transaction
To convert a floating exchange-rate regime into a fixed regime
To obtain an official revaluation from the monetary authority
x: Hedging involves covering exchange-rate risk, and a forward contract can fix the exchange rate today for a transaction to be settled in the future.

s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes spot and forward exchange rates?
o: A spot rate is for immediate delivery, whereas a forward rate is agreed now for delivery on a future date
A forward rate is determined only after the future delivery date
A spot rate is agreed today for future delivery, whereas a forward rate is for immediate delivery
Both rates necessarily relate only to cash transactions settled on the same day
x: A spot rate applies to immediate delivery, while a forward rate is fixed by agreement today for settlement at a specified future date.

s: What does an indirect exchange-rate quotation express?
o: Units of domestic currency per one unit of foreign currency
Units of foreign currency per one unit of domestic currency
The trade-weighted value of the domestic currency
The inflation-adjusted value of the domestic currency
x: An indirect quote gives foreign units per one domestic unit; a direct quote gives domestic units per one foreign unit.

s: Within how much time is a spot exchange-rate transaction settled?
x: The spot rate is for immediate delivery, with settlement within two days.

s: What is taking an open position on expected exchange-rate moves, rather than covering risk, called?
x: Hedging covers exchange-rate risk; speculation is an open position on expected moves.

s: What is covering exchange-rate risk through a forward contract called?
x: Hedging covers exchange-rate risk, for example by an importer's forward contract; speculation keeps an open position.

s: About how many months of import cover did India's forex reserves of about $701.4 billion provide?
x: Reserves of approximately $701.4 billion were associated with import cover of about 11 months.

s: In which year did the RBI institute the SAARC Currency Swap Framework?
x: The framework (2012) offers short-term BoP liquidity through bilateral swaps with the RBI, with a 3-month tenor rollable twice.

s: Whose rupee accounts are Special Rupee Vostro Accounts (SRVAs)?
o: Indian banks maintained with foreign banks
Foreign banks maintained with banks in India
The RBI with foreign central banks
x: SRVAs are rupee accounts of foreign banks with Indian banks, enabling INR trade settlement; since 2025 surplus balances may go into corporate bonds and CPs.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Masala bond — Yuan-denominated bond issued in China
Samurai bond — Yen-denominated bond associated with Japan
Panda bond — Rupee-denominated bond issued in India
Masala bond — Dollar-denominated bond issued in the United States
x: A Samurai bond is associated with the yen and Japan. Masala bonds are rupee-denominated bonds issued abroad, while Panda bonds are associated with the yuan and China.

s: Into which of the following was the INR trade settlement mechanism incorporated?
x: The INR trade settlement framework introduced by the RBI in July 2022 was built into the Foreign Trade Policy 2023.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Nostro – foreign bank's account with a domestic bank
Vostro – foreign bank's account with a domestic bank
x: Vostro ('yours') is a foreign bank's account with a domestic bank; Nostro ('ours') is a domestic bank's account with a foreign bank.

s: The Indian rupee symbol ₹ was adopted on 15 July 2010. Who designed it?
x: The symbol ₹ was adopted on 15 July 2010 and was designed by D. Udaya Kumar.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about masala bonds?
o: They are rupee-denominated bonds issued abroad, with currency risk on the investor.
Maharashtra was the first Indian State to issue them.
The name was given by the IFC.
The first masala bonds were listed on the Luxembourg Stock Exchange.
x: Kerala (2019), not Maharashtra, was the first State to issue masala bonds.

s: Which country made the first INR drawdown under the SAARC framework?
x: The first INR drawdown under the SAARC framework was made by the Maldives in April 2026.

s: What is the tenor of a swap under the SAARC Currency Swap Framework?
x: SAARC swaps are short-term BoP liquidity: a 3-month tenor, rollable twice.

s: Who issued the first masala bond in November 2014?
x: IFC issued the first masala bond in Nov 2014 and named it; Kerala was the first state (2019).

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Masala bond – Rupee, issued in India
x: Masala = rupee bond issued abroad; Samurai = yen (Japan); Panda = yuan (China).

s: Which was the first Indian state to issue a masala bond (2019)?
x: Kerala became the first state to issue a masala bond in 2019.

s: Where is SWIFT, the cooperative messaging network for cross-border payment instructions, based?
x: SWIFT (1973) is a Belgium-based cooperative; it sends payment messages but does not move funds.

s: Who issued the Resurgent India Bonds in August 1998?
x: SBI issued the Resurgent India Bonds on 5 August 1998 in US dollar, pound sterling and Deutsche Mark.

s: Under the SAARC Currency Swap Framework 2024-27, what is the size of the INR window?
x: The 2024-27 framework has a ₹250 bn INR window plus a $2 bn USD-euro facility.

s: In which year did the RBI put in place the framework for invoicing and settling international trade in rupees?
x: The RBI's INR trade settlement framework came in July 2022 and was built into FTP 2023.

s: Since 2025, in which instruments may surplus balances in Special Rupee Vostro Accounts be invested?
x: Since 2025, SRVA surplus balances may go into corporate bonds and CPs.

s: How many of the 27 European Union member states use the euro?
x:
The printed options did not include the correct answer (21); it is added as option 5.
20 until 2025 — now 21, Bulgaria having adopted the euro on 1 Jan 2026 (ECB press release, 1 Jan 2026)
Bulgaria adopted the euro on 1 January 2026, so 20 was the figure until 2025 (now 21 of the 27 EU states).

s: Ngultrum is the currency of which country?
x: Bhutan's currency is the ngultrum; Maldives uses the rufiyaa.

s: In which year was the rupee symbol (₹) introduced?
x: The rupee symbol came in 2010, after current account convertibility (1994), the First Tarapore Committee (1997) and FEMA (2000).

s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Revaluation – Official raising of the currency's value under a fixed regime
Depreciation – Market rise in the domestic-currency price of foreign currency
Devaluation – Official raising of the currency's value under a fixed regime
Appreciation – Market fall in the domestic-currency price of foreign currency
x: Devaluation is the official lowering, not raising, of a currency's value under a fixed regime; official raising is revaluation.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about exchange-rate terminology?
o: Depreciation under a floating regime means more domestic currency per unit of foreign currency.
Depreciation and appreciation are officially ordered changes under a fixed regime.
Appreciation under a floating regime means less domestic currency per unit of foreign currency.
Official changes under a fixed regime are devaluation and revaluation.
x: Depreciation and appreciation are market-driven changes under a flexible regime; official changes under a fixed regime are devaluation and revaluation.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Official increase in currency value – Revaluation
Official reduction in currency value – Depreciation
Market-driven fall in currency value – Devaluation
Market-determined currency value – Fixed exchange rate
x: An official rise is revaluation; an official cut is devaluation, a market-driven fall is depreciation and a market-set value is a floating rate.

s: If the exchange rate changes from $1 = ₹96 to $1 = ₹94 through market forces, what has happened to the rupee?
x: Fewer rupees per dollar means the rupee has gained value; a market-driven rise is appreciation, not revaluation.

s: In which year was the rupee devalued from ₹4.76 to ₹7.50 per US dollar?
x: This devaluation was in June 1966; the others were September 1949 (with sterling) and July 1991 (two steps).

s: In how many steps was the July 1991 devaluation of the rupee carried out?
x: It was about 18% in two steps, on 1 and 3 July 1991 - the last formal devaluation.

s: By about what percentage was the rupee devalued in June 1966?
x:
Many books quote 57.5% (the rise in the dollar's rupee price). Strictly the rupee was devalued by 36.5% (Spectrum p.690), the same measure as 1949's 30.5%.
In June 1966 the rupee went from ₹4.76 to ₹7.50 per US dollar: the rupee lost about 36.5% of its value, while the dollar's rupee price rose 57.5%. Measured like 1949's 30.5%, the devaluation is about 36%.

s: By about what percentage was the rupee devalued in September 1949?
x: India's first devaluation, in September 1949 along with sterling, was about 30.5%.

s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The rupee was devalued in 1949, 1966 and 1991.
Devaluation makes domestic exports relatively cheaper abroad.
The rupee was devalued twice in 1991, on July 1 and July 2.
In 1991, devaluation occurred in two steps on July 1 and July 3.
x: Option C is incorrect: in 1991 the rupee was devalued in two steps, on 1 and 3 July, not 1 and 2 July. Earlier devaluations were in 1949 and 1966.

s: To which factor does the Purchasing Power Parity theory primarily link the long-run exchange rate?
o: Volume of domestic currency notes alone
Number of foreign banks in a country
Size of the stock market alone
x: In the long run, the inflation differential between countries is a key exchange-rate anchor under Purchasing Power Parity theory.

s: Under a flexible exchange-rate system, by what is the exchange rate determined?
x: Under a flexible system demand and supply set the rate; under a fixed system the government fixes it and the RBI intervenes.

s: In a managed float, how is the exchange rate set?
o: Fixed permanently by a constitutional provision
Determined only by the price of gold
Determined by the market, with central-bank intervention when necessary
Set exclusively by commercial banks without government influence
x: In a managed float, market forces determine the rate, while the central bank may intervene directly through forex transactions or indirectly through interest rates.

s: Which of the following is correctly matched with the post-Bretton Woods classification of exchange-rate regimes?
o: Fixed — currency unions and currency boards
x: Post-Bretton Woods classifications place currency unions and currency boards under fixed regimes. Bands and crawling pegs are intermediate, while managed and independent floats are flexible regimes.

s: What kind of exchange-rate arrangement did Argentina have from 1991 to January 2002?
x: Argentina's currency board (1991-Jan 2002) is a fixed-regime arrangement.

s: Under a fixed (pegged) exchange-rate system, how is the exchange rate maintained?
o: By market demand and supply alone
By the government fixing the rate and the central bank buying or selling foreign currency to hold it
By the IMF setting daily rates
x: Under a peg the government fixes the rate and the central bank buys or sells foreign currency so that demand and supply balance at that rate.

s: Which of the following combinations represents the three elements of the Impossible Trinity?
o: Flexible exchange rate, capital controls and fiscal surplus
Fixed exchange rate, free capital flows and independent monetary policy
Fixed exchange rate, trade surplus and gold convertibility
Independent monetary policy, zero inflation and balanced budget
x: The Impossible Trinity states that a country cannot simultaneously maintain a fixed exchange rate, free capital flows and an independent monetary policy.

s: Large capital inflows tend to make a country's currency:
x: Inflows raise demand for the domestic currency and push its value up, an effect linked with Dutch disease.

s: How does a hawkish monetary-policy stance or a repo-rate hike mainly support the rupee?
o: Eliminating the current account deficit automatically
x: A hawkish stance or higher repo rate can attract carry-trade capital by improving the relative return on rupee assets, thereby supporting the currency.

s: What is deliberate undervaluation of a currency, as alleged in the case of China, criticised as?
x: Deliberate undervaluation of a currency to gain trade advantages is criticised as currency manipulation.

s: Which of the following is identified as a set of long-run determinants of the exchange rate?
o: Daily spot intervention by the central bank
Purchasing power parity, savings-investment balance and the current account
x: Long-run exchange-rate determinants include PPP, the savings-investment balance and the current account.

s: Higher imports may be accompanied by currency stability or appreciation when supported by:
x: Net investment inflows can finance imports, so higher imports do not always cause depreciation.

s: High inflation and a large fiscal deficit tend to ____ a currency's exchange value.
x: Both inflation and a fiscal deficit can weaken a currency's exchange value.

s: By what other name is the Impossible Trinity known?
x: The impossible trinity is the Mundell-Fleming trilemma: fixed rate, free capital and independent monetary policy cannot coexist.

s: With which phenomenon are large capital inflows causing currency appreciation linked?
x: Large inflows cause appreciation, linked with Dutch disease; currency manipulation is deliberate undervaluation.

s: When did FEMA, which replaced FERA, come into force?
x: FEMA was proposed in the 1997-98 Budget and came into force on 1 June 2000.

s: In which year was the second Tarapore Committee, on Fuller Capital Account Convertibility, appointed?
x: Tarapore II was appointed on 20 March 2006 and reported on 31 July 2006; Tarapore I was 1997.

s: In which Union Budget was the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) first proposed?
x: FEMA was proposed in the 1997-98 Budget, enacted in 1999 and in force from 1 June 2000.

s: What does the Reserve Tranche Position of a country in the IMF refer to?
o: The share of SDRs allocated to private commercial banks
The total amount of gold held by the country
The portion of the IMF quota that can be drawn without conditions
The country’s annual export earnings deposited with the IMF
x: The reserve tranche is the part of a member country’s IMF quota that it can draw without conditionality.

s: The Reserve Tranche Position (RTP) was historically known by which name?
x: The reserve tranche was once called the 'gold tranche', because it was paid in gold. 'Paper gold' means the SDR.

s: In September 2026, which country did India overtake to become the world's fourth-largest holder of foreign exchange reserves?
x: With reserves of $785.71 billion in September 2026, India became the fourth-largest holder after overtaking Russia.

s: With what is the rise in the share of gold in India's foreign exchange reserves principally associated?
o: Replacement of SDRs by domestic tax revenue
A prohibition on holding foreign currencies
x: The increased share of gold has been associated with diversification of India's foreign exchange reserves.

s: In which year did the IMF create Special Drawing Rights, popularly called 'paper gold'?
x: SDRs were created in 1969 under the IMF's First Amendment (agreed in 1967).

s: Which of the following is NOT included in the SDR basket?
x: The SDR basket contains the US dollar, euro, Chinese renminbi, Japanese yen and pound sterling. The Indian rupee is not included.

s: What was the Special Drawing Right (SDR), created by the IMF in 1969, meant to do?
o: Replace the US dollar in trade
Fix the world price of gold
x: The SDR is an IMF reserve asset created in 1969 to supplement member countries' official reserves.

s: When was the largest general allocation of SDRs, about $650 billion, made?
x: The largest general SDR allocation (SDR 456 bn, about $650 bn) was in August 2021.

s: Since when has the SDR basket of the IMF included the renminbi?
x: The five-currency basket including the renminbi applies since 1 Oct 2016 (decided 2015).

s: Which is the smallest component of India's foreign exchange reserves?
x: The order by share is FCA > Gold > SDRs > Reserve Tranche Position, so the RTP is the smallest.

s:
Consider the following statements about Special Drawing Rights (SDRs):
1. SDRs exist only as book-keeping entries in IMF records.
2. The Indian rupee is one of the currencies in the SDR basket.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: SDRs are book-keeping entries; the basket has the dollar, euro, renminbi, yen and pound, but not the rupee.

s: What is the India-Japan Bilateral Swap Arrangement renewed from 28 February 2026?
o: A gold-backed loan facility without currency exchange
A one-way transfer of rupees to Japan
A two-way arrangement involving local currencies against US dollars
A multilateral arrangement among all SAARC members
x: The India–Japan Bilateral Swap Arrangement is a two-way facility involving the exchange of local currencies against US dollars, renewed from 28 February 2026.

s: Who acts as the custodian of India's foreign exchange reserves?
x: The Reserve Bank of India is the custodian of India's foreign exchange reserves.

s: With which of the following was the Bretton Woods system of 1944 primarily associated?
o: Floating rates based entirely on private speculation
A universal currency managed by the WTO
Fixed exchange rates centred on the dollar
Independent floating of all national currencies
x: The Bretton Woods system of 1944 established fixed exchange rates centred on the dollar and was associated with the IMF and World Bank.

s: In which year was the Smithsonian Agreement signed?
x: The Smithsonian Agreement was in 1971, after Bretton Woods (1944) and before India's 1991 devaluation and 1993 unification.

s: What happened to the Indian rupee in September 1975?
o: Made fully floating without any intervention
Pegged to gold under the Smithsonian Agreement
Delinked from pound sterling and pegged to a basket of currencies
Linked exclusively to the US dollar
x: In September 1975, the rupee was delinked from pound sterling and pegged to a basket of currencies.

s: When did India accept IMF Article VIII and move to current account convertibility?
x: India accepted Article VIII in August 1994, after the dual rates were unified on 1 March 1993.

s: Which of the following statements regarding the IMF is incorrect?
o: India joined the IMF on 27 December 1945.
The IMF was conceived at the Bretton Woods Conference of 1944.
The IMF was formally established on 27 December 1944.
The IMF was formally established on 27 December 1945.
x: Option C is incorrect: the IMF was formally set up on 27 December 1945, after being planned at Bretton Woods in 1944. India was a founding member.

s: When were India's dual exchange rates under LERMS replaced by a unified rate?
x: LERMS came in 1992-93, the unified rate on 1 March 1993, and current account convertibility in August 1994.

s: Which exchange-rate system did India follow from 1947 to 1971?
o: Par value system under the IMF
x: 1947-1971 was the par value system under the IMF; the basket peg came in Sept 1975.

s: How many nations took part in the Bretton Woods Conference of July 1944?
x: 44 nations met at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, 1-22 July 1944.

s: What is India's share in the IMF's SDR quota (March 2026)?
x: India's quota is 2.75% of SDR quota; its vote share is 2.63%.

s: Which country became the 191st member of the IMF in October 2024?
x: Liechtenstein joined the IMF as its 191st member in October 2024.

s: Where was the Bretton Woods Conference of July 1944 held?
x: The Bretton Woods Conference (1-22 July 1944, 44 nations) was held in New Hampshire, USA.

s: What is the primary aim of RBI intervention in the foreign exchange market?
o: Defend a permanently fixed rupee-dollar level
x: The RBI intervenes mainly to curb volatility, using reserves if needed, not to defend a fixed rate.

s: What happened to the rupee in FY 2025-26 up to January 2026?
x: The rupee depreciated by 5.4% in FY 2025-26 up to January and was among the most depreciated currencies, along with the yen.

s: In the context of offshore Non-Deliverable Forward markets, which measure is used by the RBI to reduce speculative pressure on the rupee?
o: Abolishing all forward contracts in India
Restricting domestic banks’ participation in offshore NDF markets and enforcing Net Open Position limits
Permitting unlimited offshore positions by domestic banks
x: The RBI restricts domestic banks’ offshore NDF participation and enforces Net Open Position limits to curb speculative pressure and volatility.

s: Which of the following is a Government structural measure rather than an RBI exchange-rate tool?
o: Selling dollars in the spot market
x: Import curbs and export promotion are Government structural measures. Spot intervention, NOP limits and dollar-rupee swaps are associated with RBI action.

s: Which of the following combinations was associated with the rupee crossing ₹96.2 per US dollar on 19 May 2026?
o: Brent crude near $110 and FPI outflows exceeding ₹2 lakh crore
A sharp increase in official interest rates and a trade surplus
A fall in imports and a rise in gold exports
Brent crude near $50 and strong FPI inflows
x: On 19 May 2026, the rupee crossed ₹96.2 per dollar amid Brent crude near $110 and FPI outflows of more than ₹2 lakh crore.

s: What do banks do in a dollar-rupee buy/sell swap?
o: Buy dollars from the RBI and sell them back later at a discount
Sell dollars to the RBI permanently
Buy rupee bonds from the RBI
Sell dollars to the RBI and buy them back later at a premium
x: Banks sell dollars to the RBI and repurchase later at a premium, injecting rupee liquidity without permanently altering reserves.

s: Till 30 September 2026, the RBI bore the full hedging cost on fresh deposits under which scheme?
x: The RBI bore the full hedging cost on fresh FCNR(B) deposits till 30 Sep 2026.

s: What does a rise in the Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) tend to do?
x: A rising REER means real appreciation, which tends to reduce export competitiveness.

s: What does a rise in the rupee's Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER) indicate?
x: A rise in NEER means rupee appreciation, making imports cheaper and exports less competitive.

s: How is a high REER generally interpreted for the rupee?
o: Convertible only on the capital account
Fixed permanently to the US dollar
x: A high REER generally indicates an overvalued rupee. Since REER incorporates relative inflation, it is a better indicator of competitiveness than NEER alone.

s: For what is the NEER adjusted to obtain the Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER)?
x: REER is NEER adjusted for relative price or inflation differentials between domestic and foreign economies.

s: What is the base year of the RBI's NEER and REER indices?
x: NEER/REER are on base 2015-16 = 100.

s: For baskets of how many currencies are the RBI's trade-weighted NEER/REER indices compiled?
x: RBI publishes 40-currency and 6-currency indices; the 6-currency index has a moving base.

s: Which of the following about the WTO is NOT correct?
o: It was established under the Marrakesh Agreement of 1994
It came into being on 1 January 1994
x: The WTO came into being on 1 January 1995, not 1994, under the Marrakesh Agreement signed in 1994; it replaced the GATT and is headquartered in Geneva.

s: Which agreement, signed in April 1994, created the WTO?
x: The Marrakesh Agreement (April 1994) created the WTO.

s: Who is the Director-General of the World Trade Organization?
x: The WTO, headquartered in Geneva, is headed by Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala; India is a founding member of both GATT and the WTO.

s: Which of the following situations illustrates the national-treatment principle under WTO rules?
o: A country gives an export subsidy to domestic firms.
A country grants the same tariff concession to every foreign trading partner.
An imported product, after entering the domestic market, is treated like a similar domestic product for internal taxation and regulation.
A country imposes a quantitative restriction on all imports.
x: National treatment requires imported goods to be treated like domestic goods once they have entered the market, particularly in internal taxation and regulation. Equal treatment among foreign trading partners is the MFN principle.

s: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala is which Director-General of the WTO?
x: She is the 7th DG and first woman; Roberto Azevedo was the 6th.

s: Which country became the 164th member of the WTO in July 2016?
x: Afghanistan became the 164th member on 29 July 2016; Nepal was 147th and Serbia is only an observer.

s: Under which WTO principle must a trade advantage given to one partner be extended to all WTO partners?
x: MFN means non-discrimination among partners; national treatment means treating imports like domestic goods once inside.

s: Along with the IMF and the World Bank, which body is called the third pillar of the world economy?
x: The WTO is the third pillar of the world economy with the IMF and the World Bank.

s: As of April 2026, the World Trade Organization had how many members?
x: The WTO had 166 members as of April 2026. 123 was the number of contracting parties in the Uruguay Round (and India was the 123rd member to accept the Fisheries Subsidies Agreement); 164 and 150 are older or wrong membership figures.

s:
Assertion (A): The WTO replaced the GATT.
Reason (R): The WTO is an international trade organization.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
x: Both are true: the WTO replaced GATT, and it is an international trade organisation. Being an organisation does not explain why it replaced GATT, so R does not explain A.

s: Trade-related investment measures are covered by which WTO agreement?
x: TRIMS covers investment measures; TRIPS covers IPR, GATS services and SPS/TBT health and technical standards.

s: On what does India rely for geographical-indication protection?
o: The Lisbon Agreement, of which it is a founding member
The Lisbon Agreement, applied only to farm exports
TRIPS, as it is not a member of the Lisbon Agreement
The Lisbon Agreement in preference to TRIPS
x: India is not a member of the Lisbon Agreement on appellations and prefers TRIPS for GI protection.

s: Under the WTO Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures (SCM), how are subsidies for research and development, regional development and environmental purposes classed?
x: The SCM Agreement groups subsidies as prohibited (the 'red light' category), actionable (open to countervailing duty) and non-actionable (R&D, regional and environmental). Amber Box is an Agreement on Agriculture category for trade-distorting farm support, not an SCM class.

s: Which Indian legislative measure introduced product patents to comply with the TRIPS Agreement?
o: The Geographical Indications of Goods Act, 1999
The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006
The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers’ Rights Act, 2001
x: India amended its Patents Act in 2005 to introduce product patents in accordance with TRIPS requirements.

s: In which year did India ratify the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement?
x: The TFA came with the Bali package (2013); India ratified it in 2016.

s: What does the Information Technology Agreement (ITA, 1996) of the WTO provide for?
x: ITA gives zero duty on IT products; TRIPS sets IPR standards and TFA simplifies customs.

s: Under the SCM Agreement, what are 'red light' subsidies?
x: SCM classes subsidies as prohibited (red light), actionable and non-actionable; there is no Red Box in the AoA.

s: On whose recommendation was India's Patents Act, in force from 1972, based?
x: The Patents Act came into force in 1972 on the basis of the N. Rajagopala Ayyangar Committee (1957).

s: Which Indian law is linked to the WTO SPS and TBT agreements on food safety and standards?
o: Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001
x: India's compliance with SPS/TBT is through the Food Safety and Standards Act 2006.

s: Which organisations set up the Codex Alimentarius Commission in 1963?
x: The Codex Alimentarius Commission was set up by FAO and WHO in 1963; the WTO uses its food-safety standards.

s:
Consider the following statements about the GATT:
1. It was signed on 30 October 1947.
2. It had 23 founding contracting parties.
3. It was signed at Marrakesh.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: GATT was signed at Geneva (not Marrakesh) on 30 October 1947 by 23 founding contracting parties.

s: When did India become a member of GATT?
x: India joined GATT on 8 July 1948 and is a founding member of both GATT and the WTO.

s: The Uruguay Round, launched at Punta del Este in 1986, was which round of GATT negotiations?
x: The Uruguay Round was the eighth GATT round, launched at Punta del Este in September 1986 and concluded in 1993 with 123 contracting parties.

s: The Dunkel Draft contained proposals for the agreements of which round of trade negotiations?
x: The Dunkel Draft was made up of proposals by Arthur Dunkel, GATT Director-General and Chair of the Trade Negotiations Committee, for the Uruguay Round agreements.

s: GATS, TRIPS and TRIMS extended trade rules beyond goods as a result of which GATT round?
x: The Uruguay Round expanded the framework beyond goods through GATS, TRIPS and TRIMS.

s: How many contracting parties took part in the Uruguay Round?
x: The Uruguay Round had 123 contracting parties; 23 were GATT's founders and 166 is today's WTO membership.

s: When was the Dunkel Draft (Draft Final Act) of the Uruguay Round tabled?
x: Arthur Dunkel, GATT Director-General, tabled the Draft Final Act on 20 December 1991.

s: In which year was the Uruguay Round of GATT negotiations concluded?
x: The Uruguay Round ran from 1986 to 1993; the Marrakesh Agreement followed in April 1994.

s:
Consider the following statements about the GATT and the WTO:
1. The WTO has a broader multilateral trade framework than the GATT.
2. The WTO covers goods, services, intellectual property rights and investment measures.
3. The GATT mainly dealt with goods.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: All are true: the WTO is wider than GATT because it covers goods, services, IPR and investment, while GATT dealt mainly with goods.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about subsidy boxes under the WTO Agreement on Agriculture?
o: Amber Box covers price- or quantity-linked support such as MSP, measured as AMS.
Blue Box covers direct payments under production-limiting programmes.
Green Box support is not trade-distorting and has no limits.
Blue Box support is subject to reduction commitments.
x: Blue Box payments are exempt from reduction commitments.

s: The Agreement on Agriculture (AoA) rests on which of the following three pillars?
o: Domestic support, market access and export competition
Market access, investment protection and government procurement
Export competition, services and industrial subsidies
Domestic support, intellectual property and trade facilitation
x: The AoA has three pillars: domestic support, market access and export competition.

s: The de minimis limit for agricultural domestic support is what percentage of production value for developed and developing countries, respectively?
x: The de minimis limit is 5% of production value for developed countries and 10% for developing countries.

s: Under the WTO Agreement on Agriculture, what is the conversion of non-tariff barriers into tariffs called?
x: This is tariffication; developed countries were then to cut tariffs by 36% over 6 years.

s: Which of the following is NOT an official subsidy box under the Agreement on Agriculture?
x: Green, Blue and Amber are the subsidy boxes under the AoA. Red, Orange and Yellow are not AoA boxes; a prohibited-subsidy category described as a red-light category belongs to the SCM context.

s: Under the AoA, by how much did developed countries have to cut Total AMS?
x: Total AMS cut was 20% over 6 years for developed and 13.3% for developing countries.

s: Blue Box payments may be based on what share of base production, or less?
x: Blue Box payments are on fixed areas and yields, on 85% or less of base production, or a fixed number of livestock.

s: Under tariffication, by how much did developing countries have to cut tariffs?
x: Tariff cuts were 36% over 6 years for developed and 24% over 10 years for developing countries.

s: Which of the following falls in the Green Box under the Agreement on Agriculture?
x: Research, disease control and infrastructure are non-distorting Green Box support; MSP and input subsidies are Amber Box.

s: Under the Agreement on Agriculture, by how much did developed countries have to cut export subsidies over six years?
x: Developed countries had to cut export subsidies by 36% in value or 21% in volume over 6 years from 1986-90 levels.

s: At which Ministerial Conference was the WTO Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies adopted?
x: MC12 at Geneva (June 2022) adopted the Fisheries Subsidies Agreement and a COVID-related TRIPS waiver.

s: At which Ministerial Conference was the WTO Trade Facilitation Agreement concluded as part of the Bali package?
x: The TFA came from the Bali package at MC9 (2013); India ratified it in 2016.

s: Where was the first WTO Ministerial Conference held?
x: MC1 was at Singapore (1996), MC2 Geneva (1998), MC3 Seattle (1999) and MC4 Doha (2001).

s: At which Ministerial Conference was the Doha Development Agenda launched?
x: MC4 at Doha (2001) launched the Doha Development Agenda and adopted the TRIPS-public health declaration.

s: With which WTO Ministerial Conference was the elimination of agricultural export subsidies associated?
x: The Nairobi Ministerial Conference of 2015 adopted the outcome concerning elimination of agricultural export subsidies.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: MC11 (Buenos Aires) – Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies
MC10 (Nairobi) – Launch of the Doha Development Agenda
MC12 (Geneva) – Elimination of agricultural export subsidies
x: The Bali Ministerial Conference (MC9, 2013) produced the Bali Package, including the Trade Facilitation Agreement and an interim Peace Clause on food stockholding.

s: At the WTO MC14 at Yaoundé (2026), India blocked the addition of which plurilateral agreement to Annex 4?
x: At MC14 India blocked adding the Investment Facilitation for Development (IFD) plurilateral agreement to Annex 4, although 129 of 166 members backed it.

s: The Fourteenth WTO Ministerial Conference (MC14), held in March 2026, took place at which of the following places?
x: WTO MC14 was held at Yaoundé, Cameroon, from 26 to 29 March 2026.

s:
Arrange the following WTO events in chronological order:
A. MC12 adopted Phase 1 of the Fisheries Subsidies Agreement.
B. MC9 adopted the Peace Clause for food-security stockholding.
C. MC14 was held at Yaoundé.
D. MC13 was held at Abu Dhabi.
x: The correct order is MC9 in 2013, MC12 in 2022, MC13 in 2024 and MC14 in 2026.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the 14th WTO Ministerial Conference at Yaounde (March 2026)?
o: It produced only a draft 'Yaounde package' and no ministerial declaration.
A permanent solution on public stockholding was achieved.
The e-commerce moratorium lapsed on 31 March 2026.
Sixty-six members signed a separate E-Commerce Agreement barring duties on digital trade.
x: The permanent public-stockholding solution remained deadlocked at MC14.

s: The WTO Ministerial Conference, its highest decision-making body, must meet at least once every:
x: Under the Marrakesh Agreement the Ministerial Conference meets at least once every two years.

s: At which Ministerial Conference was the WTO customs-duty moratorium on electronic transmissions begun?
x: MC2 at Geneva in 1998 began the e-commerce moratorium.

s: Duty-free quota-free access for LDCs was agreed at which WTO Ministerial Conference?
x: MC6 at Hong Kong (2005) agreed to end farm export subsidies and gave duty-free quota-free access for LDCs.

s: Where was the WTO Ministerial Conference that collapsed amid protests in 1999 held?
x: MC3 at Seattle (1999) collapsed amid protests; Cancun (2003) also collapsed.

s: Which WTO Ministerial Conference was held at Buenos Aires in 2017?
x: MC11 was held at Buenos Aires in 2017; it ended with no declaration.

s: Which of the following is NOT one of the 'Singapore issues' raised at the first WTO Ministerial Conference (1996)?
x: The Singapore issues were investment, competition, transparency in procurement and trade facilitation.

s: At which WTO Ministerial Conference was the COVID-19 TRIPS waiver adopted?
x: MC12 at Geneva (June 2022) adopted the COVID TRIPS waiver along with the Fisheries Subsidies Agreement.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: G-33 – African Group, ACP and LDCs
G-90 – Food security and special products
NAMA-11 – Developing countries on non-agricultural market access
x: NAMA-11 is a group of developing countries, including India, concerned with non-agricultural market access. The G-90 is the African Group, ACP countries and LDCs.

s: What does the G-33, formed in 2003 during the Doha process, mainly focus on?
o: Interests of the African Group, ACP and LDCs
Food security, Special Safeguard Mechanism and special products
x: The G-33 is a group of 40-plus developing countries, including India, focused on food security, the Special Safeguard Mechanism and special products.

s: Which countries make up the G-90 group at the WTO?
o: 40+ developing countries focused on food security
The African Group, ACP countries and LDCs
x: G-90 = African Group + ACP countries + LDCs; G-33 focuses on food security, NAMA-11 on industrial goods.

s: What does the Special Safeguard Mechanism sought by developing countries at the WTO allow?
o: Raising tariffs for a short time against import surges or price falls
x: The SSM lets developing countries raise tariffs briefly when imports surge or prices fall; G-33 pushes for it.

s: From disputes concerning which matter does the Peace Clause adopted at Bali in 2013 protect developing countries?
o: Trade in banking and insurance services
x: The Bali Peace Clause shields developing-country public stockholding programmes from disputes until a permanent solution is found.

s: Which country first invoked the WTO Peace Clause for rice in 2020?
x: India was the first country to invoke the Peace Clause for rice in 2020.

s: India argues that its MSP procurement for the National Food Security Act is counted as an Amber Box subsidy using which price?
x: India's public stockholding grievance is that MSP procurement is treated as Amber Box support calculated against an outdated historical reference price.
